items.text: Sami is playing with the red car. Layan wants it too. Can they find a plan without grabbing?
Layan says: I want to play. Sami says: I want to finish the garage. Let us hear both needs.
Ask calmly: May I have a turn when you finish? Choose the need you want to act out.
Agree on an ending signal, or play with two cars. Choose a plan that suits you both. You can ask for another idea.
Try the plan with real toys or puppets. Then choose: We tried our agreement.
Did the plan suit you both? Keep it, change it, or take a break.
Agree on the end of the turn. When the car enters the garage, Sami offers Layan a turn. We do not grab.
Each child chooses a car and a road. Play together without a forced swap. Change the plan if it does not feel right.
يَلْعَبُ سَامِي بِالسَّيَّارَةِ الْحَمْرَاءِ، وَتُرِيدُهَا لَيَانُ أَيْضًا. هَلْ نَجِدُ حَلًّا دُونَ سَحْبِ اللُّعْبَةِ؟
تَقُولُ لَيَانُ: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَلْعَبَ. وَيَقُولُ سَامِي: أُرِيدُ إِكْمَالَ الْمِرْآبِ. لِنَسْمَعِ الْحَاجَتَيْنِ.
اسْأَلْ بِهُدُوءٍ: هَلْ يَأْتِي دَوْرِي عِنْدَمَا تَنْتَهِي؟ اخْتَرِ الْحَاجَةَ الَّتِي تُرِيدُ تَمْثِيلَهَا.
نُحَدِّدُ نِهَايَةَ الدَّوْرِ، أَوْ نَلْعَبُ بِسَيَّارَتَيْنِ. اخْتَرَا حَلًّا يُنَاسِبُكُمَا. يُمْكِنُ طَلَبُ بَدِيلٍ أَوْ مُسَاعَدَةٍ.
جَرِّبَا الِاتِّفَاقَ بِلُعْبَةٍ أَوْ دُمْيَتَيْنِ. يَحِقُّ لَكُمَا طَلَبُ اسْتِرَاحَةٍ. اضْغَطَا جَرَّبْنَا بَعْدَ الْمُحَاوَلَةِ فَقَطْ.
هَلْ أَرَاحَكُمَا الِاتِّفَاقُ؟ إِنْ نَاسَبَكُمَا نَحْفَظُهُ، وَإِلَّا نُعَدِّلُهُ. الْمُهِمُّ أَنْ نَسْمَعَ بَعْضَنَا.
نَتَّفِقُ عَلَى نِهَايَةِ الدَّوْرِ. عِنْدَمَا تَدْخُلُ السَّيَّارَةُ الْمِرْآبَ، يَعْرِضُ سَامِي الدَّوْرَ عَلَى لَيَانَ. لَا نَنْتَزِعُ اللُّعْبَةَ.
يَخْتَارُ كُلُّ طِفْلٍ سَيَّارَةً وَطَرِيقًا. نَلْعَبُ مَعًا بِدُونِ تَبْدِيلٍ إِجْبَارِيٍّ. وَإِنْ لَمْ نَرْتَحْ نُعَدِّلُ الْحَلَّ.
Omar wants the basket farther away. Hana wants a distance she can manage. Can they change the rule together?
Omar wants a challenge. Hana wants a comfortable way to join. Both needs matter.
Ask: Can we test the new distance together before deciding?
Try a short test round, or let each player choose a suitable distance. Explore both plans.
Try your chosen rule with a soft ball or act it out with toys. Then confirm that you tried it.
Did everyone get to join? Keep the rule or change one part and test again.
Try the new distance in a short round. Afterwards, ask each partner whether the change suited them.
Choose a suitable distance for each player. A fair game can include different distances. Ask whether the plan feels right to everyone.
تُرِيدُ هَنَا إِبْعَادَ السَّلَّةِ، وَيُفَضِّلُ عُمَرُ قُرْبَهَا. هَلْ نُغَيِّرُ الْقَاعِدَةَ مِنْ غَيْرِ اتِّفَاقٍ؟
تُرِيدُ هَنَا تَحَدِّيًا جَدِيدًا. وَيُرِيدُ عُمَرُ دَوْرًا يُنَاسِبُهُ. نَسْمَعُ كُلَّ طَرَفٍ قَبْلَ اخْتِيَارِ الْحَلِّ.
نَقُولُ: مَا رَأْيُكَ أَنْ نُجَرِّبَ؟ ثُمَّ نَنْتَظِرُ الْجَوَابَ. يَحِقُّ لِصَدِيقِنَا الرَّفْضُ أَوِ اقْتِرَاحُ بَدِيلٍ.
نُجَرِّبُ جَوْلَةً ثُمَّ نُرَاجِعُهَا، أَوْ يَخْتَارُ كُلُّ لَاعِبٍ مَسَافَةً تُنَاسِبُهُ. أَيُّ الْحَلَّيْنِ تُرِيدَانِ تَجْرِبَتَهُ؟
جَرِّبَا بِكُرَةٍ لَيِّنَةٍ فِي مَكَانٍ آمِنٍ مَعَ الْمُرَافِقِ، أَوْ مَثِّلَا الْمَوْقِفَ بِالدُّمَى. نَتَعَلَّمُ دُونَ مُقَارَنَةٍ.
هَلْ شَارَكَ كُلٌّ مِنْكُمَا بِرَاحَةٍ؟ إِنْ كَانَتِ الْقَاعِدَةُ مُتْعِبَةً، نُقَرِّبُ السَّلَّةَ أَوْ نُعَدِّلُ الِاتِّفَاقَ.
نُجَرِّبُ جَوْلَةً قَصِيرَةً بِمُوَافَقَةِ اللَّاعِبَيْنِ. ثُمَّ نُقَرِّرُ: هَلْ نُكْمِلُ، أَمْ نُغَيِّرُ الْمَسَافَةَ، أَمْ نَعُودُ لِلْقَاعِدَةِ الْأُولَى؟
يَخْتَارُ كُلُّ لَاعِبٍ مَسَافَةً تُنَاسِبُهُ. قَدْ نَخْتَلِفُ فِي الطَّرِيقَةِ، وَنَحْتَرِمُ الدَّوْرَ، وَنَسْتَمْتِعُ بِاللَّعِبِ مَعًا.
Adam and Reem are building a bridge. Zaid wants to join. Can they find a useful role without knocking down the work?
Zaid wants to help build. Adam and Reem want to keep their bridge safe. Listen to both needs.
Ask: What can I build with you? Show me which part needs help.
Zaid could build the road or another part of the bridge. Ask what he would like to try.
Build a small part together, then test the bridge with a toy car. Confirm only after you try.
Did Zaid have a useful role? Did everyone agree? Change the jobs if needed.
Zaid chooses to build the road. Show where it meets the bridge and leave him a real building job. Ask whether it suits him.
Choose a part of the bridge that Zaid wants to build. Explain how it connects. Then the group tests the car together.
يَبْنِي آدَمُ وَرِيمٌ جِسْرًا، وَيُرِيدُ زَيْدٌ الِانْضِمَامَ. كَيْفَ نَجِدُ دَوْرًا مُفِيدًا وَنَحْتَرِمُ مَا بَنَاهُ أَصْحَابُنَا؟
يُرِيدُ زَيْدٌ أَنْ يَلْعَبَ مَعَهُمَا. وَيُرِيدُ آدَمُ وَرِيمٌ إِكْمَالَ الْجِسْرِ. لَدَيْنَا حَاجَةُ الِانْضِمَامِ وَحَاجَةُ إِكْمَالِ الْعَمَلِ.
اسْأَلْ: مَا الدَّوْرُ الَّذِي أُشَارِكُ بِهِ؟ لَا نَهْدِمُ عَمَلَ غَيْرِنَا، وَلَا نَفْرِضُ دَوْرًا لَا يَرْتَاحُ لَهُ.
يُمْكِنُ لِزَيْدٍ بِنَاءُ الطَّرِيقِ، أَوِ الْمُشَارَكَةُ فِي بِنَاءِ الْجِسْرِ. وَيُمْكِنُ اقْتِرَاحُ دَوْرٍ آخَرَ. أَيُّ اتِّفَاقٍ تُرِيدُونَ تَجْرِبَتَهُ؟
مَثِّلُوا الْأَدْوَارَ بِمُكَعَّبَاتٍ كَبِيرَةٍ أَوْ دُمْيَاتٍ. هَلْ دَوْرُ كُلِّ لَاعِبٍ وَاضِحٌ؟ يُمْكِنُ طَلَبُ تَبْدِيلٍ أَوِ اسْتِرَاحَةٍ.
هَلْ وَجَدَ كُلُّ لَاعِبٍ دَوْرًا مُفِيدًا؟ إِنْ لَمْ يَرْتَحْ أَحَدٌ، نَسْمَعُهُ وَنُعَدِّلُ الدَّوْرَ، أَوْ نَخْتَارُ نَشَاطًا آخَرَ.
يَخْتَارُ زَيْدٌ بِنَاءَ الطَّرِيقِ. نُرِيهِ أَيْنَ يَتَّصِلُ بِالْجِسْرِ، وَنَتْرُكُ لَهُ عَمَلًا حَقِيقِيًّا. نَسْأَلُهُ إِنْ كَانَ يُنَاسِبُهُ.
يُضِيفُ زَيْدٌ قِطْعَةً إِلَى الْجِسْرِ، وَيَبْنِي صَدِيقَاهُ الطَّرِيقَ وَيَخْتَبِرَانِ الْمُرُورَ. يُمْكِنُ تَبَادُلُ الْأَدْوَارِ بِرِضَا الْجَمِيعِ.
Sami and Layan each want to colour an apple. They have one red pencil.
One partner says: I want to colour my apple. The other says: I want to finish my picture.
May I use the pencil after this part?
Compare both plans. Choose what suits you both, or ask for another idea and help. Agreement is a choice.
Colour two apples and try your way of sharing the pencil.
Did both of you finish a part? If waiting was too long, make each turn smaller.
Colour a small part, then offer the pencil to your partner.
One draws a green leaf while the other colours an apple. Then swap jobs.
Layan wants to roll the ball. Sami wants to hold it a little longer.
One partner says: I want to roll the ball. The other says: I need time to get ready.
I am ready. May I roll it to you?
Try passing the ball along the floor in a clear space.
Did the ball arrive gently? You can move closer together.
Ask whether your partner is ready, then roll the ball gently.
Roll the ball around a cushion, then send it to your partner.
Layan chooses an animal book. Sami chooses a vehicle book.
One partner says: I want animal pictures. The other says: I want vehicle pictures.
I like this book. Which one do you like?
Open both books and try your choice with your grown-up.
Did each of you find a picture you like? You can change the plan.
Take turns looking at one page from each book.
Choose an animal and a vehicle, then make up a journey for them.
Playtime is ending. Layan wants to put away animals, while Sami collects blocks.
One partner says: I want to sort the animals. The other says: I need help with the blocks.
Will you help me with this part?
Try your plan with a small set of toys.
Did the jobs suit both of you? You may ask for more help.
Each partner puts one kind of toy into its box.
Put the animals away together, then move on to the blocks.
Sami is on the swing. Layan waits at a safe distance and wants a turn.
One partner says: I want to finish my turn. The other says: I want to know when my turn starts.
When does your turn end? I will wait here.
Act out a swap with a toy, or try it with an adult supervising.
Was the turn signal clear? Change it if you need to.
Agree on the end of the turn with your grown-up. Swap only when the swing stops.
Choose chalk drawing while waiting. Your grown-up calls when it is your turn.
Layan has the castle mould. Sami wants to build a castle too.
One partner says: I want to finish the tower. The other says: I want to build a castle.
May I have the mould after this tower?
Build two parts of the castle and try swapping jobs.
Did both of you contribute? You can change the jobs.
Finish one tower, then offer the mould to your partner.
One partner fills the mould while the other makes a sandy bridge.
Sami chooses the star sticker. Layan wants that same star.
One partner says: I want the star. The other says: I want a star for my card.
I want this star. Can we find another idea?
Make one card or two after both of you agree.
Did the arrangement suit you both? Nobody has to accept the alternative.
One chooses the sticker. The other draws a star if that feels fair to them.
Put the star on a card that you make together.
Layan wants to hold the watering can. Sami wants to water the plant.
One partner says: I want to hold the can. The other says: I want to water the plant.
Shall we choose a job for each of us?
Try two jobs with a grown-up. Stop before adding too much water.
Did the water reach the soil? Did both jobs suit you?
Take turns watering two plants, using the amount your grown-up shows you.
One carries the light can. The other points to the plant's soil.
Sami holds the last piece. Layan wants to place it after helping with the puzzle.
One partner says: I want to place the piece. The other says: I want to finish what I helped build.
Can we finish in a way that suits us both?
Try the plan with a puzzle that has only a few pieces.
Did you enjoy building together, or only placing the last piece?
One points to the space. The other places the piece after you agree.
Finish this picture, then rebuild a small part so your partner can finish it.
Layan wants to sit on the cushion. Sami is resting there.
One partner says: I want a comfortable place. The other says: I need to finish resting.
Is there another comfortable place for me?
Sit in two comfortable places, or act this out with toys.
Did each of you find comfort? Rest is not a competition.
Look with your grown-up for another cushion nearby.
Choose the reading mat and let your partner keep their resting place.
Sami builds a long track. Layan wants to use the curved piece.
One partner says: I want to finish the track. The other says: I want to make a bend.
Can we try this piece in two places?
Move the train along the track and try your agreement.
Did each of you have a part in building?
Add the bend to one track that you build together.
Try the bend in one track, then in the other, after agreeing.
Layan wants the toy chair for her puppet. Sami is using it for a bear.
One partner says: I want a seat for the puppet. The other says: I want the bear to keep its seat.
Could we make another seat?
Act out a short visit with the puppet and bear.
Did both toys find a place in the game?
Build a second seat from large blocks.
The bear sits first, then visits the puppet and leaves the chair for it.
Layan wants the scarf for a captain role. Sami chose it for his journey.
One partner says: I want a costume for my role. The other says: I want to finish my journey.
Can we find something for each role?
Act out two short scenes with safe costume pieces.
Did each of you keep a role you enjoy?
Make a paper badge for one role and leave the scarf for the other.
Swap the scarf after a short scene you agree on.
Sami is making play dough balls. Layan wants the same roller.
One partner says: I want to roll my dough. The other says: I want to finish my shape.
Can we roll one piece for each of us?
Make two shapes and try the option you agreed on.
Did you make two shapes you both like?
Roll one small piece, then pass the roller.
One uses the roller. The other may flatten dough with a palm if they choose.
The block box is close to Sami. Layan cannot reach it comfortably.
One partner says: I want blocks I can reach. The other says: I want to keep building.
Can we put the box between us?
Build two towers and try reaching the pieces.
Is reaching easier now? Move the materials again if needed.
Move the light box where both of you can reach it.
Put blocks on two trays and exchange pieces when needed.
Sami is explaining his building. Layan wants to show him her picture.
One partner says: I want to finish my thought. The other says: I want you to see my drawing.
When you finish, will you listen to my idea?
Try a short conversation about two things you made.
Were both ideas heard? For urgent help, call an adult straight away.
Give a quiet signal. Wait for the thought to end, then speak.
Put the drawing beside the building and describe each one in turn.
Sami likes Layan's special puppet. Layan wants to keep it with her.
One partner says: I want to try the puppet. The other says: I want to keep my puppet.
May I borrow it? You can say no.
Use two toys to act out asking to borrow and respecting the answer.
Did we respect the boundary? Sharing does not mean making someone give in.
Respect the no and choose another shared toy.
Layan may show her puppet if she wants. It stays in her hands.
Sami accidentally touched the tower and it fell. Layan needs space and help.
One partner says: I want to help repair it. The other says: I need space before rebuilding.
I am sorry that happened. Would you like my help now?
Act this out with a small tower and clear permission.
Did the repair help? Hugs or immediate forgiveness are never required.
Wait until Layan agrees, then rebuild one part together.
Offer nearby pieces if she wants them, and give her space.
Layan wants a lively rhythm. Sami prefers a quiet tune.
One partner says: I want a lively rhythm. The other says: I want a quiet tune.
Can we find a rhythm that suits us both?
Try a short rhythm. Stop whenever either partner asks.
Was the sound comfortable for both of you? Playing quietly is an option too.
Try a short part of each choice at a comfortable volume.
Make a simple rhythm together with gentle claps.
Omar wants a tall bridge. Hana wants it wide enough for the car.
One partner says: I want a tall bridge. The other says: I want my car to pass.
Can we test the width before adding height?
Roll a car under the bridge. Change one piece if needed.
Did the bridge include both ideas? Describe what you changed.
Build a wide base, test the car, then make the bridge taller.
Build two small bridges and compare how steady they are and whether the car fits.
Omar and Hana both want to be the seller in their pretend shop.
One partner says: I want to arrange the shop. The other says: I want to serve the shopper.
Which part of being the seller do you enjoy?
Act out two orders with pretend goods and play money.
Did both of you try the job you enjoy?
One partner sells one order, then you swap roles.
One arranges the goods. The other serves a puppet customer.
Hana wants a blue sea. Omar plans a city on the same sheet.
One partner says: I want space for the sea. The other says: I want space for my city.
Shall we connect our ideas or use two sheets?
Draw two small parts. Ask before changing your partner's drawing.
Did each person keep their idea?
Choose space for a sea and a city, then connect them with a road.
Draw on separate sheets, then place them side by side if you want.
Omar wants to try the drum. Hana wants to hear a quiet story.
One partner says: I want to try a rhythm. The other says: I need less noise.
The sound is too loud for me. Can we change the place or time?
Try a gentle sound, or act out the plan without drumming.
Is reading comfortable now? Stop if the sound is still uncomfortable.
Have a short gentle rhythm time, then stop for the story.
Your grown-up helps find a rhythm space away from the reading area.
Hana wants the puppet to go home. Omar wants it to go on a trip.
One partner says: I want a calm ending. The other says: I want a story adventure.
Could we act out both ideas before choosing?
Try the endings with puppets and a block house.
What did each partner's idea add to the story?
The puppet takes a short trip, then returns home.
Act out the story twice, with a different ending each time.
Omar is building a car road. Hana wants room for a station.
One partner says: I want a connected road. The other says: I want an entrance to my station.
Can we test an entrance that keeps the road connected?
Move a car from the start to the station.
Is the road connected, and can the car reach the station?
Add a side road to the station without removing the first route.
Place the station near the road's end, then test the car's arrival.
Hana wants a quiet rabbit home. Omar adds a large dinosaur.
One partner says: I want space for the rabbit. The other says: I want room for the dinosaur.
How could we make room for both animals?
Move both toys and test the entrances and space.
Is there room for both toys without knocking down your partner's work?
Build two neighbouring homes with a path between them.
Make a shared yard and a separate corner for each toy.
Omar wants to draw the shapes. Hana wants to choose colours and draw too.
One partner says: I want to draw the shapes. The other says: I want to draw and choose colours.
Shall we swap jobs or draw two parts?
Make a small picture that includes work from both of you.
Did both of you get to draw and choose colours?
One draws a shape and the other colours it. Then swap jobs.
Each draws and colours a part. Then connect the two parts.
Omar's pieces fill the table. Hana needs space for her project.
One partner says: I need to keep my pieces. The other says: I need room to work.
Can we arrange the pieces without damaging your work?
Make a small part and test the space for hands and tools.
Does the space work for both of you now?
Put pieces you are not using onto a nearby tray.
Agree on two work areas and move materials with permission.
Omar wants a fast race. Hana prefers moving more slowly.
One partner says: I want to move quickly. The other says: I want a comfortable pace.
Can we choose a game we can both join comfortably?
Try a short route in a safe space with your grown-up.
Did both of you find a comfortable way to join?
Carry a soft ball on a cloth and walk together.
Choose suitable distances and review the rule without teasing.
Hana wants the flower path. Omar wants the tree path in their pretend park.
One partner says: I want to see the flowers. The other says: I want to reach the trees.
Can we draw a journey that visits both places?
Move a toy along the park map you drew.
Did the toy visit what matters to each of you?
Draw a route past the flowers and trees before returning.
Choose two short journeys and take turns choosing where to start.
Omar wants to collect everything quickly. Hana wants to sort the materials.
One partner says: I want a clear floor. The other says: I want to find the tools later.
What do we need first to make the space comfortable?
Tidy a small corner, then try finding one tool.
Is the walkway clear, and is the tool easy to find?
Collect materials in a safe basket, then sort them together.
One clears the walkway while the other sorts the table materials.
Hana needs the large tongs. Omar is using them to move pieces.
One partner says: I want to move pieces. The other says: I need the tongs for building.
How many pieces do you need before I use the tongs?
Build a small part with large pieces and safe tongs.
Did the tongs help both projects, or should the turn be shorter?
Agree on a small job, then pass the tongs.
One moves the pieces the other requests, then you swap jobs.
Hana wants the lamp for her paper bird. Omar wants it for his tree.
One partner says: I want the bird to appear. The other says: I want the tree to appear.
Can we try a position that shows both shapes?
Try two shadows with a safe lamp set up by your grown-up.
Did both ideas appear? You can change the positions.
Arrange the bird and tree so both appear on the screen.
Show two short scenes and take turns holding the shapes.
Hana wants a seat where she can see pictures. Omar wants to sit near his friend.
One partner says: I need to see the book. The other says: I want to sit near my friend.
Can we move the cushions so everyone can see?
Arrange toy seats, then check whether everyone can see the picture.
Could everyone see the picture without excluding anyone?
Arrange the cushions in a half circle without blocking the book.
Bring the book closer to each partner after a page.
Omar wants to introduce the story. Hana wants to ask questions with the pretend microphone.
One partner says: I want to introduce it. The other says: I want to ask questions.
Shall we make room for a question after the introduction?
Act out a short interview without recording or filming.
Did we hear an introduction and a question? Pointing can replace speaking.
Introduce one short idea, then pass the pretend microphone for a question.
Each partner gives part of the introduction, then signals for a question.
Hana wants to try another game. Omar wants to keep building with her.
One partner says: I want to try another activity. The other says: I want to keep building.
I want to change activities. How can we leave our work safely?
Act out ending a shared activity with clear, respectful words.
Did we respect the choice to stop and look after the work?
Put the building in a safe place, then each choose an activity.
Hana explains her part. Omar may continue without changing it.
Hana wants to help Omar build. He wants to try it himself.
One partner says: I want to help. The other says: I want to try it myself.
Would you like a hint, or shall I wait beside you?
Try offering one kind of help after asking permission.
Did the person trying still get to do the work?
If Omar asks, Hana describes where the piece goes. He places it himself.
Hana waits without touching the work. Omar asks for help if he needs it.
Tidy-up time is near. Omar and Hana want to keep their unfinished project.
One partner says: I want to keep what I built. The other says: I want to remember our next step.
Can we choose what to keep and what to put away?
Choose a small part to keep, or draw its plan.
Can we tell what the next step will be when we return?
Put the project on a safe tray and put unused pieces away.
Draw the project and its next step, then put the pieces away.
Reem suggests a ball rule. Adam and Zaid do not understand it yet.
One partner says: I want to start the game. The other says: I want to understand what to do.
Could we show the rule before we start?
Try a short round without scores. Stop to ask questions.
Could everyone explain their step? Change anything that is still unclear.
Show one slow round. Each player explains what they will do.
Draw simple picture steps, then try them together.
Adam wants a short route. Reem wants a challenge. Zaid asks about the clues.
One partner says: I want a route I can finish. The other says: I want a fun clue I can understand.
Can we choose a challenge with a way to get help?
Look for a toy in a clear, safe area with your grown-up.
Did the plan help everyone join without getting lost?
Make a clear main route and a harder optional branch.
Take turns reading picture clues, searching and holding the map.
The team wants to build a town, but there are only a few long blocks.
One partner says: I need blocks for a road. The other says: I need blocks for a roof.
What does each idea need in order to work?
Build a small house and road and test whether the pieces are enough.
Was the reason for sharing clear? Fair does not always mean equal numbers.
Give each part what it needs and find alternatives for decorations.
Try one small build, then reuse the pieces in another.
It is time to move on. Adam wants to finish the bridge. Reem and Zaid are getting ready.
One partner says: I want to keep what I started. The other says: I need to get ready to move on.
What small step could help us keep our plan now?
Practise a short transition while keeping a part or a plan.
Do we know what to return to? Do not promise a time that cannot happen.
Put the important part on a tray and return the other materials.
Draw what remains and agree on a possible return time with your grown-up.
Adam suggests every step. Reem and Zaid want to try leading too.
One partner says: I want to try my idea. The other says: I want a chance to suggest the plan.
Could we try leadership that listens to everyone?
Build a small route and try changing the leader or sharing decisions.
Were all ideas heard? Leading does not remove anyone's right to say no.
Each partner leads a short round and asks the others what they think.
Share decisions about the space, materials and starting point.
The group suggests a touching game. Zaid does not want that kind of play.
One partner says: I want a group game. The other says: I do not want touching in the game.
I do not want touching. Can we find another way?
Try a no-touch signal game and respect anyone's choice to stop.
Did the right to say no stay clear after the agreement?
Use a hand signal from a distance instead of touching.
Zaid may choose another role or a separate activity without pressure.
Adam said something that upset Reem. Reem needs space before returning.
One partner says: I want to repair what I said. The other says: I need space and safety.
I understand my words upset you. What help would feel right now?
Act out the conversation with puppets without repeating the hurtful words.
What change will we see in the next game?
Explain what words you will change, then wait until your partner is ready.
Ask your grown-up to support a safe conversation without requiring forgiveness.
The team makes a noisy toy route. Someone nearby is reading quietly.
One partner says: We want to test the route. The other says: Someone else needs quiet.
How can we play without making the space uncomfortable?
Try one short test and ask whether the people nearby are comfortable.
Did the sound change enough? If not, plan again.
Put the toy route on a mat that softens the sound.
Move the route to a safe space suited to this activity.
The game needs a high reach. Zaid prefers to play sitting down.
One partner says: We want a fun game. The other says: I want to join from a comfortable position.
Could we change the materials instead of leaving a player out?
Try joining large pieces from comfortable positions.
Can everyone take a real part rather than a token role?
Place the target within reach. Each player chooses a comfortable position.
Turn the idea into a table game everyone can reach.
The team planned outdoor play, but the grown-up says rain makes the area unsuitable.
One partner says: I want to keep our plan. The other says: I want something we can do now.
Which part of our idea can we keep?
Build a small version of the route in a safe indoor space.
What did we keep from the idea, and what did we change?
Turn the route into a map with toys on the floor.
Save the plan for a possible later time and choose an indoor activity.
Adam promised to build with Reem and tell a story with Zaid at the same time.
One partner says: I am waiting for our plan. The other says: I need to explain what is possible.
I made two plans for the same time. Can we plan again?
Act out the two promises with puppets and a plan you can actually carry out.
Is the plan clear now, or did we make another unclear promise?
Agree on a possible order for the activities. Either partner may decline.
If everyone agrees, make the building the setting for the story.
The team plans a town. They disagree about starting with roads, a park or houses.
One partner says: I want to start my part. The other says: I want a plan that supports every part.
What do the other parts need before we build?
Build a tiny town with a few parts and test how they connect.
Did the order help everyone's work? Why keep it or change it?
Prepare the base and path, then build the parts you each chose.
Each partner builds a small model, then agree on how to connect them.
Reem wants a memory of the building. Zaid does not want his picture included.
One partner says: I want to remember our project. The other says: I do not want my picture taken.
Can we keep a memory without pictures of people?
Act out both choices with a paper frame. This app does not need a camera.
Did we respect the no and avoid sharing anyone's image?
Draw the building on paper without photographing anyone.
If everyone wants it, the grown-up may photograph just the building, without people.
The team finds a toy under the table. They do not know who owns it.
One partner says: I want to find the owner. The other says: I want to keep the toy safe.
Who can help us return it?
Practise returning a toy with a puppet and a lost-property box.
Is the toy safe, with a clear way to return it?
Give the toy to your grown-up and explain where you found it.
With your grown-up's guidance, put it in the known lost-property place.
Adam shows the town the team built. Reem's and Zaid's work has not been mentioned.
One partner says: I want to show the project. The other says: I want my contribution to be seen.
Could we describe what each partner added?
Show a small project to a puppet or your grown-up.
Were contributions recognised without ranking the people who made them?
Each partner shows their part with words or pointing.
Prepare a shared description of the parts and everyone's contributions.
The rule removes a player after a mistake. Zaid has been waiting a long time.
One partner says: I want a clear challenge. The other says: I want another chance to join.
Can we keep the challenge and reduce the waiting?
Try aiming soft balls at a nearby basket.
Is the challenge still interesting, with everyone taking part?
Each player gets another try after their partner's turn.
Add your attempts towards a shared goal without removing anyone.
Zaid suggests a new passage. Reem and Adam want to keep the old route.
One partner says: I want to try my idea. The other says: I want to keep what already works.
Can we test the idea without dismantling the original?
Move the toy through both routes and describe what happened.
What evidence helps us keep the change or put the piece back?
Build a small model beside the route, then compare how toys move through it.
Agree to change one piece and keep a way to put it back.
Reem wants a park project. Adam and Zaid want a boat harbour.
One partner says: I want to build the park idea. The other says: I want to build a place for boats.
Do we need one project, or could we make two neighbouring parts?
Build two small parts and test the space and sharing plan.
Did we keep a respectful relationship without forcing one shared idea?
Build a park beside a harbour and choose a link between them.
Agree how to share materials and work on two projects without teasing.
The team agreed on jobs, but Zaid still waits most of the time.
One partner says: I want to finish my work. The other says: I want a role that really happens.
What actually happened after our agreement?
Try the revised agreement in a short building round.
What changed in the waiting time and chance to take part?
Make each task shorter and try swapping sooner.
Choose useful tasks that everyone can do at the same time.
Listen to each partner and compare two plans. Try your agreement, then review it. You may stop or ask for help.
Say what you need and ask a grown-up for help. Agreement is a choice. Every partner may say no.
Take a break. You do not have to keep playing now. Return when you are ready.
We saved an agreement we tried. We can return to it and change it when our needs change.
I am your teacher. We will watch situations and listen to ideas. This is a demonstration. Afterwards, choose a situation and try it yourself.
Let us look at a new situation. Think about each partner’s needs without forcing a solution.
